The apparent academic mystery is a wordplay on "courses." The student was not registering for classes; they were choosing menu courses (dishes) for a formal banquet dinner organized by their residential hall or student society, and had to submit their menu selections before the organizer's deadline. Another person (the host/organizer, or the banquet staff acting on the student's signal) was the deliberate human agent involved. At the dinner, the multi-course meal was served to the protagonist. Over the course of the evening the protagonist ate every course themselves; no one else ate those courses, and the food was not taken away, spoiled, or given to others before eating. When the plates were empty, the protagonist deliberately signaled the serving staff to clear them, so the dishes were carried off. Thus, by the end of that single evening, every one of the student's chosen "courses" had vanished—simply because they had been eaten and the empty plates cleared—rather than because of any course-registration problem, system error, or cancellation.

The puzzle turns on a wordplay: "courses" here are not university classes but the dishes of a multi-course meal. The student was attending a formal banquet dinner (such as a residential-hall or student-society high-table dinner), where each attendee must submit their menu choices (e.g., which soup, main, dessert) in advance before a set RSVP/menu deadline. The student did this—those were "my courses." At the banquet, the courses were served to the student at the table. The student ate some of the food but could not finish all of it because they became full/didn't want more. Rather than let the remaining food sit, the student deliberately signaled the serving staff to clear the plates, and a staff member carried the unfinished courses away. Thus, by the end of that single evening, every one of the student's chosen "courses" had disappeared—partly eaten and partly cleared from the table—not because of any course-registration failure, system error, capacity shortage, or cancellation. The "deliberate action by another person" in the story is the banquet staff (and the host/organizer who arranged and paid for the dinner) carrying out the serving and clearing; the "deadline" was the pre-dinner menu-selection deadline.

Were the individual courses, as a matter of routine banquet service, taken away one after another during the evening (each course replaced by the next) rather than all left on the table until the end?

The mystery is a wordplay on "courses." The student was not registering for classes; they were choosing the menu dishes (the "courses") for a formal banquet dinner—such as a residential-hall or student-society high-table dinner—and had to submit those menu choices before the organizer's selection/RSVP deadline. At the banquet, the meal was served course by course to the protagonist, sitting as a guest. The protagonist ate some of each course but became full and did not finish everything. Because a banquet is served in sequence, the serving staff routinely cleared each course from the table to make way for the next one, so course after course was carried away through the evening. By the end of that single evening, every one of the student's chosen courses had disappeared—eaten in part and cleared away by the staff as the dinner progressed—not because of any course-registration failure, system error, limited capacity, or cancellation. The "deliberate action by another person" is the waiting staff carrying out the routine course-by-course service and clearing.

The trick is the double meaning of "courses": here they are the dishes of a dinner, not university classes. The student had to choose their menu courses in advance—before the organizer's selection deadline—for an organized dinner (a hall/society meal) that they attended. At the meal the food was individually plated and served one course at a time. The student ate part of each course but did not finish everything: the plates still had uneaten food on them because the dishes simply were not to the student's taste (not because they were too full, and not because the food was objectively spoiled or badly cooked). Serving staff, following the normal course-by-course service—bringing the next course and removing the previous one, also acting on the student's signal to clear—deliberately carried the courses away one after another. By the end of that single evening, every one of the student's chosen courses had disappeared: some of it had been eaten, and the uneaten remainder had been cleared away by the staff as the dinner progressed. The "deliberate action by another person" is the serving side of the event clearing each course; nothing went wrong with class registration, the enrolment system, course capacity, or any cancellation.

The riddle rests on a double meaning of "courses": they are not university classes but the dishes of a meal. The student personally chose, in advance and before a deadline, which dishes would be served at a dinner they attended—a university/hall/society organized meal. At the dinner the food was individually plated and served one course at a time. The student ate part of the courses but did not finish everything: uneaten food was still on the plates when they were cleared. The reason was not that the portions were too large or that the student was too full, and not that the food was spoiled or badly cooked; the dishes simply were not to the student's taste, so the student stopped eating them. In the normal course of a served dinner the waiting staff brought each next course and removed the previous one, acting as well on the student's signal to clear the plates. So, course by course, the staff deliberately carried the food away. By the end of that one evening every one of the student's chosen courses had vanished: some had been eaten and the remaining uneaten portions had been cleared away by the serving staff. That staff clearing is the "deliberate action by another person," and the advance menu choice is the "deadline." Nothing went wrong with class registration, the enrolment system, course capacity, or any cancellation—the "courses" were merely the dinner's dishes, eaten in part and cleared away over a single evening.
